strengths: High-quality, large-scale dataset with 20K real-world demonstrations from 95 users, rich contextual information (screenshots, accessibility trees, user profiles, temporal/location data) enabling research on mobile LLM agents

Well-executed practical data collection methodology with functioning Android app, multiple quality control measures, and longitudinal collection over one month covering 506 apps and 40+ intent categories

Comprehensive evaluation framework with two complementary tracks addressing both proactive prediction and personalized execution, thorough ablations, and evaluation on diverse models (both generalist and GUI-specific)
Strong reproducibility and transparency: detailed appendices, ethics statement with privacy measures, explicit prompts, and commitment to open-sourcing code and data
Insightful ablation studies (Table 11) demonstrating importance of contextual components (time being most critical) and reasonable out-of-domain generalization analysis
Addresses important and timely problem of making mobile LLM agents more proactive and personalized rather than purely reactive
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—primarily a benchmark and dataset contribution without novel algorithms, architectures, or LLM agent designs; task formulations (Eq. 1-2) are straightforward standard LLM applications

Extremely low absolute performance (12.8% SR for proactive, 38.5% for personalized) without sufficient analysis of why models fail or how to substantially improve; fine-tuning yields only modest gains (3.1%→9.7%, 1.5%→12.5%); lack of error analysis limits insights

Critical geographic/demographic limitation: all 95 users from mainland China using Chinese third-party apps, raising serious questions about generalizability to other regions and global mobile app ecosystems

Evaluation methodology concerns: textual similarity metrics may not capture semantic equivalence; binary success metrics provide no partial credit; human baseline is weak (only 20 annotators, not systematic); inter-annotator agreement not reported

Insufficient analysis of results: no deep investigation of the massive model-human performance gap; limited analysis of what models actually learn or when they succeed/fail; missing error categorization and failure mode analysis

Task formulation questions: inferring intent from few screenshots is inherently ambiguous; no discussion of inter-annotator agreement on ground truth; formulation may not align with how humans approach the task

Presentation and scope limitations: critical details relegated to appendices; human study methodology underdeveloped; limited discussion of practical applicability given low success rates; no computational cost analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing gap between passive task execution and proactive, personalized mobile agents
Substantial real-world data collection effort: 20K episodes from 95 users over one month with rich contextual information
Thoughtful benchmark design with two complementary task tracks (proactive suggestion and personalized execution)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple model families with extensive ablations and supplementary experiments
Commitment to reproducibility with promised open-sourced code, data, and detailed methodological appendices
weaknesses: Severely limited geographic and linguistic generalizability: all data collectors from mainland China using primarily Chinese apps, undermining applicability to global audiences
Extremely low absolute performance numbers raise practical utility concerns: 12.8% best proactive task SR and 38.5% personalized execution SR are concerning even with fine-tuning
Limited methodological novelty for top-tier venue: paper is primarily a dataset/benchmark contribution with no novel algorithms, architectures, or learning methods beyond standard LoRA fine-tuning
Questionable evaluation metrics: textual similarity threshold (0.3) appears ad-hoc without justification; no validation that metrics correlate with actual user satisfaction
Insufficient human evaluation for a benchmark paper: only 200 episodes for metric validation; unclear how 30.3% human baseline was computed; no study validating practical utility
Privacy concerns under-addressed: real user screenshots containing location, activity, and profile data pose significant re-identification risks despite anonymization claims
Incomplete experimental analysis lacking error analysis by intent/app type, investigation of which user attributes influence behavior, and breakdown of systematic failure modes
Weak connection between two proposed tracks: Section A.6.2 shows minimal transfer learning between tracks, raising question of necessity of both tasks
Overstated claims in abstract/conclusion: describes 38.5% success rate as 'good results' and makes claims about leveraging user information that lack deep validation
Presentation issues: dense with scattered results, unclear mathematical notation, limited intuitive explanation of why these tasks challenge modern LLMs

strengths: Novel benchmark introducing two new evaluation dimensions (proactive task suggestion and personalized task execution) that fill important gaps in mobile LLM agent evaluation
Large-scale, high-quality longitudinal dataset: 21,437 episodes from 95 users collected over one month with rich contextual information (location, time, user profiles, action sequences)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 10+ models with thorough ablation studies examining task difficulty, contextual factors, and fine-tuning effects
Careful methodology with proper data splits preventing user/app/intent leakage, and out-of-domain generalization analysis
Extensive supplementary experiments and analysis (A.6) including human validation of metrics (Table 13)
Promised open-source release with detailed documentation supporting reproducibility
Well-written with clear motivation and good visualizations of problem formulation and data statistics
weaknesses: Limited geographic and linguistic scope: all 95 contributors from mainland China using only Chinese third-party apps; generalizability to other regions and app ecosystems unclear, which is critical for a top-tier venue

Concerningly low absolute performance: best model achieves only 12.8% success rate for proactive suggestion vs 30.3% human performance; 38.5% for personalized execution. This 17.5% gap raises questions about task formulation and feasibility

Minimal error analysis and insights: no qualitative investigation of failure modes, limited case studies, and superficial analysis of which task categories are hardest and why; limited proposals for improvement

Evaluation metric concerns: requiring exact step-level action matching for personalized task success (SR₂) is extremely strict; similarity metric (Sim₁g₂) depends on pre-trained embeddings with limited robustness validation; human evaluation only on 4 models
Pure benchmark paper with no algorithmic or methodological novelty: all experiments use standard approaches (prompt-based LLMs, LoRA fine-tuning) without proposing solutions to identified challenges
Limited fine-tuning scope: only LoRA on one model (Qwen-2.5-VL-7B) with 16K training episodes; improvements modest (3.1%→9.7% still <10%); unclear if larger models would benefit

Reproducibility concerns: uses anonymous link (cannot verify access), requires custom FingerTip app for data collection, privacy anonymization procedures insufficiently detailed for sensitive mobile data

Insufficient justification for two-track design: limited analysis of why proactive suggestion and personalized execution should be separate vs unified tasks; transfer learning experiments (Table 9) presented without deep interpretation
Ethical considerations underexplored: continuous app usage monitoring enables significant user tracking/manipulation risks; privacy-preserving alternatives not discussed despite sensitivity of data
